Zeal for God's House
zēl fôr gŏdz hous
n. phrase (the consuming zeal of Psalm 69, applied to Christ at the cleansing of the temple)
Greek zelos, heat, fervour, jealousy for something. The psalm's verb is eat up — a zeal that consumes the man who has it.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

“And his disciples remembered that it was written, The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up” (John 2:17), recalled as He drove out the money-changers with a scourge of small cords (John 2:15). The quotation is Psalm 69:9: “For the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up; and the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me” — a psalm Paul also applies to Christ (Rom 15:3). The Lord's charge against the traders is Jeremiah's: “It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves” (Mat 21:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines zeal as passionate ardor in the pursuit of any thing; in general, ardor in the pursuit of good, or in the maintenance of a cause; and warns that it may be ill-directed.

expand to see more

ZEAL, n. Passionate ardor in the pursuit of any thing. In general, zeal is an eagerness of desire to accomplish or obtain some object, and it may be manifested either in favor of any person or thing, or in opposition to it.

It is usually applied to religion or to some good cause, but it may be applied to a bad object.

ZEALOUS, a. Warmly engaged or ardent in the pursuit of an object.

Key Scripture

John 2:17 — "And his disciples remembered that it was written, The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up."

John 2:15 — "And when he had made a scourge of small cords, he drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen; and poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables;"

Psa 69:9 — "For the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up; and the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me."

Mat 21:13 — "And said unto them, It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves."

Rom 15:3 — "For even Christ pleased not himself; but, as it is written, The reproaches of them that reproached thee fell on me."

Modern Corruption

The cleansing of the temple is borrowed to justify a temper, and the psalm says the zeal consumed the One who had it.

expand to see more

This is the passage angry Christians reach for, and the borrowing usually fails on three counts. The zeal is for God's house, not for the man's own honour — Christ was silent under personal insult and violent only about His Father's courts. It was deliberate rather than sudden: John says He made a scourge of small cords, which takes time, and Mark records that on an earlier visit He looked round about upon all things and, the hour being late, went out to Bethany and came back the next day. And the psalm's verb points inward: the zeal hath eaten me up. It consumed Him, and He paid for it; a temper that costs its owner nothing and its neighbours a good deal is not this.

The charge He brought is worth reading in full, because the modern application usually stops at the tables. My house shall be called the house of prayer — that is Isaiah, and Isaiah's sentence continues, for all people — but ye have made it a den of thieves. The market was in the court of the Gentiles, the one place a God-fearing foreigner could pray, and it had been filled with livestock and currency exchange. The zeal was for a house whose door had been blocked, and the people blocked out of it were the outsiders.

Psalm 69 is the psalm of the reproached righteous sufferer, quoted repeatedly of Christ — they gave me vinegar to drink, they hated me without a cause, the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me. Zeal in that psalm is not an emotion but a position: standing where God's honour is being attacked and taking the blows meant for Him. That is what the disciples remembered when they watched Him with the cords, and it is why the memory is recorded not as an outburst but as a fulfilment.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek zelos (G2205), zeal, fervour; katesthio (G2719), to eat up, consume; oneidismos (G3680), reproach; Hebrew qin'ah (H7068), zeal, jealousy.

expand to see more

Greek zelos (G2205) — zeal; John 2:17, Romans 10:2, 2 Corinthians 7:11, Philippians 3:6.

Greek katesthio (G2719) — to eat up, devour; John 2:17, Mark 12:40, Galatians 5:15.

Hebrew qin'ah (H7068) — zeal, jealousy; Psalm 69:9, Isaiah 9:7, 59:17, Numbers 25:11.

Usage

"“The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up” — the verb points inward."

"“When he had made a scourge of small cords” — deliberate, not sudden."

"“My house shall be called the house of prayer” — Isaiah adds, for all people."
